messages.subject_clean: Different estimates with xHMC vs. NUTS (was: positive transformation)
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, February 9, 2016 at 4:33:15 AM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> The cusp in the Jacobian at y = 0 will cause all kinds of problems for HMC.
> But in general the pathological behavior for small x is not necessarily any
> better than the overflow for exp, so which is better depends on the context.
> Given the cusp in this one, though, I would recommend exp with an effort
> to standardize the model as much as possible.
>
> On Feb 9, 2016, at 5:38 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > I think this came up before, but I can't remember what was said. For a transformation of an unbounded parameter (x) to a positive parameter (y), we are using y = exp(x). Would it be better to do something like y = 0.5 * (sqrt(x^2 + 4) + x) whose inverse is x = y - 1 / y? This transformation does not overflow / underflow as rapidly as the exponential one. You can roundtrip negative 1 million and get back -999992.4 and can roundtrip pretty much any big positive number. There could be some numerical difficulties if a user initializes y to a really small number like 1e-9, but that seems like a lesser problem.

I finally got around to trying this transformation:

parameters {
  real x;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> y;
  y <- 0.5 * (sqrt(square(x) + 4) + x);
}
model {
  increment_log_prob(log1p(x / sqrt(square(x) + 4))); // Jacobian
  increment_log_prob(gamma_log(y, 3, 1));
}

If you bound y away from zero and use 2.9.x, then it works fine in this case:

Inference for Stan model: positive.
64 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=1000; thin=1;
post-warmup draws per chain=1000, total post-warmup draws=64000.

      mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
x     2.50    0.02 2.01 -0.93  1.16  2.30  3.65  7.00 17933    1
y     2.99    0.01 1.71  0.64  1.74  2.67  3.90  7.14 17429    1
lp__ -1.39    0.01 0.82 -3.75 -1.59 -1.07 -0.87 -0.81 15549    1

But if you use 2.10.x, y is just biased

                 Mean      MCSE  StdDev         5%    50%        95%  N_Eff  N_Eff/s     R_hat
lp__            -1.56  5.91e-03   0.979  -3.56e+00  -1.19  -8.11e-01  27483    26381  1.00e+00
accept_stat__   0.838  5.59e-03   0.198   4.17e-01  0.935   1.00e+00   1256     1206  1.01e+00
stepsize__       1.18  5.58e-04   0.141   9.88e-01   1.16   1.44e+00  64000    61434  7.31e+13
treedepth__      1.02  2.60e-03   0.144   1.00e+00   1.00   1.00e+00   3041     2919  1.01e+00
n_leapfrog__     2.02  5.16e-03    1.10   1.00e+00   1.00   3.00e+00  45283    43467  1.00e+00
divergent__     0.000  0.00e+00   0.000   0.00e+00  0.000   0.00e+00  64000    61434      -nan
energy__         2.07  7.79e-03    1.22   8.75e-01   1.71   4.51e+00  24524    23540  1.00e+00
x                2.66  1.36e-02    2.32  -7.33e-01   2.49   6.69e+00  29173    28003  1.00e+00
y                3.17  1.16e-02    1.94   6.99e-01   2.84   6.84e+00  28277    27143  1.00e+00

If there is pathological behavior, it is not very evident in the usual diagnostics. The only thing that seems weird is that treedepth__ is almost always 1.

Ben

messages.subject: paper on black-box stochastic variational inference
messages.subject_clean: paper on black-box stochastic variational inference
messages.body_plain:
Just spotted this. Cites/discusses Stan.

Black-Box Stochastic Variational Inference
in Five Lines of Python

http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~duvenaud/papers/blackbox.pdf

Several large software engineering projects have been undertaken to support
black-box inference methods. In contrast, we emphasize how easy it is to
construct scalable and easy-to-use automatic inference methods using only
automatic differentiation. We present a small function which computes stochastic
gradients of the evidence lower bound for any differentiable posterior. As an
example, we perform stochastic variational inference in a deep Bayesian neural network.

messages.body_plain:
They write, "Theano (Bastien et al., 2012), Torch (Collobert et al., 2002), and Stan Stan (2015) require learning a new syntax in which to express basic operations, essentially acting as interpreters for a restricted mini-language."
I don't know Theano, but is Stan really a restricted mini-language?  I thought it's just C+?

They write, "Autograd can handle Python code containing control flow primitives such as for loops, while loops, recursion, if statements, closures, classes, list indexing, dictionary indexing, arrays, array slicing and broadcasting."
But Stan can handle all this too, no?

Is it just that they want to work in Python, not in C++?

This does remind me, though, that I'd like to see the Stan implementation of the neural network for the digit recognition problem.  I think Daniel's writing that one up?
A

Python would be easier than in a domain-specific language like the
Stan Modeling Language.  The problem of course is that you have
to deal with the failures that arise when Autograd reaches a function
through which it can’t autodiff (or autodiff accurately).  In a very real
sense it’s a false sense of security.

messages.body_plain:
In practice, though, their program is very similar to the Stan math library, no?  The tradeoffs are:

1. Stan is easier if you know statistics, or if you know C++
2. Stan is faster
3. Stan has lots of preprogrammed probability distributions, math functions, ODE's, etc.
4. Autograd is better for certain sorts of hashing.
5. Autograd is easier if you know Python

So it depends on the importance of items 4 and 5 for the user, compared to items 1, 2, and 3.  Does that sound fair?  I feel like the paper is somewhat misleading in that it presents Autograd as being qualitatively different from Stan and these other programs, but actually they are all different versions of the same thing, just written in different languages and with different features programmed in.  Would that be a fair description?

A

Stan and Stan Math work in plain old C++.  But most of
our users use our domain-specific language (DSL), which
is C-like, but not C.

I'm pretty sure PyMC is different in that it has you
build a graphical model using predefined components, not
try to autodiff an arbitrary Python program.   I don't know
how easy it is to add components.  But it's definitely an
API you need to learn.  It's not magic.

Theano, which PyMC is using, is fundamentally different
in that it's symbolic differentiation that generates
code rather than the template overload autodiff that Stan
uses.  So they may be targeting Theano when they talk
about branching, etc., which I don't think Theano can do.
(I hate saying all this on public forums without being
sure, hence the hedging.)

Also, anything can be written in 1 line of code with
enough back-end scripting.  Like when you call ADVI
from RStan :-)

I don't know how Autograd compares to Stan in speed.

And I also agree we need to ping Daniel---wasn't he going
to write that neural net?  If he doesn't have time, I can
do it.

- Bob

Last year the entire panel largely reduced to everyone arguing that hard problems
require trading off bias for reduced variance, then my countering that you can’t do
that robustly in practice without being able to quantify the bias and variance.
Some agreed in concept but perhaps not in practice, some argued that no one has
ever done that for any algorithm so we why start now?  The conversation hasn’t
evolved much since then so I don’t really have anything new to contribute.

But if the panel this year is focused on software then maybe someone can talk about
setting up model ensembles for benchmarking algorithm accuracy and some of
the early results with Stan and ADVI.  Of course if the focus is on tools for the
applied researcher it would be great for the speaker to emphasize that applied
researchers can do only fragile work when they get nominal results without any
sense of error!

messages.subject: Putting draft pharmacometric functions on the Stan Github
messages.subject_clean: Putting draft pharmacometric functions on the Stan Github
messages.body_plain:
The original post was in an e-mail chain, but here is a summary, and answer to some of the questions that have been asked.

My team is writing new functions for Stan with applications in Pharmacometrics. These functions can be called directly inside a stan file (so there is no dependence on whether the user uses cmdStan, PyStan, etc.)

We call this function library Torsten, after Torsten Teorell, who is regarded as the father of Pharmacokinetics.

The current code is compatible with stan/math-2.10.0.

The functions are coded in C++ and would be located in a directory under stan/math. So I expect to upload them in the stan-dev/math branch. The major advantage in doing so is that it will be easier to work on the code and get help on it, since it will be accessible to the community.

To expose some of these functions, I modified rev/mat.hpp and function_signatures.h. Other functions however are higher-order functions (to the same effect as integrate_ode_bdf and integrate_ode_rk45), and cannot simply be exposed in function_signatures.h. So I edited a few grammar files for the sole purpose of exposing these higher-order functions. I expect to share these modifications using the stan-dev/stan branch.

These higher-order functions have 14 arguments, which means we will need to increase the limit on the number of arguments (which is currently 12).

I still have to write unit tests, consistent with Stan practices. (I wrote some examples and tests using cmdStan and R, for development purposes but these are likely not consistent with Stan's practices. In due time, I will upload the examples to the stan/examples repo).

I agree with Bob's suggestion: we can start with a wiki and I am happy to attend a stan meeting to discuss design.

I hope this clarifies matter, and I'm happy to answer any other question.

This is really great news and I am very curious to see the solutions you have come up with.

In fact, I intended to start such a wiki on how to make Stan better/easier to use for PK/PD.

>From my perspective we need a discussion on the design of things. I myself have come up with large Stan programs which can exactly do what I want - this is in my case to take a Nonmem data set and fit PK/PD models.

I intentionally kept things to be programmed in the Stan language only as I think that there should be no Nonmem (or PK/PD) specifics in Stan C++ and I am also not sure if we want to have PK model specifics in Stan (unless there are good arguments for it, of course).

>From my experience in programming these models I figured it would probably make sense to include an event handling mechanism in Stan. In PK models it is crucial to code the dosing history of a given patient. To me it would be natural to include into Stan a facility (functions and possibly data-structures) which can handle these events for the purpose of making it easier to code and to speedup things. Such an event mechanism will probably be very useful for other domains as well aside from PK/PD models and the event handler may not be limited to ODE models, but should be able to cope with analytic models as well.

To move forward, we should definitely discuss during a Stan meeting. I guess we also need a wiki and maybe a scratch place to keep Thorsten code around and maybe my little Stan only solution. From there we should decide how to design things, what makes sense to include into Stan itself and what should live on the Stan language side.

Sebastian

Hi Sebastian,

I'll set up a wiki so we can pool ideas, and will create a gitHub repo to post Thorsten. Once I have created the unit tests and dealt with forward auto-diff, I'll proceed to add the code to stan-dev.

Some quick thoughts:

The main benefit of using built-in stan functions is that the user does not need to write extensive code in the function block. I also imagine it would be pretty involved (if at all possible?) to write in Stan some of the code I did in C++ (I used classes and functors a lot...). Built-in functions make the coding more efficient and very easy, which I think will be key to interest users.

All the functions take in NONMEM data and return amounts in each compartment at each event. There are roughly speaking 4 functions. Here are two examples:

PKTwoCptModel() which analytically computes the solution to a two compartment model with first order absorption.

genCptModel_bdf() which computes the solution to an ODE system specified by a user using the integrate_ode_bdf function.

These functions all take advantage of exactly the same event handling mechanism, which augments the data and then sequentially predicts the amounts one event at a time. What changes from one function to the other is the function that predicts the amount at an individual event.

Right now the event mechanism is designed for NONMEM data, but I agree it would be great to generalize it. Maybe we could create a stan function that let's the user specify the one-event predictive function in the function block and then runs it sequentially through all the events.

Charles

Well, my Stan programs got ~1k lines long, but it works. So I was able to dump a NONMEM data set into Stan, then do some index fiddling to prepare the data for efficient traversal in what I call an event driver function.

A huge fraction of that code is completely agnostic to the specific model. In fact, the model function (be it an ODE or not) most be able to calculate the solutions for a given state of the compartments, the parameters and the initial time.

I was able to handle a 2-cmt oral dosing situation with time-changing clearance. It's tedious work to put that together and I guess things run faster if the event handling would be done by Stan.

For Stan I think we need a data-structure to represent events and a function to "execute" these events given a model. This would be very useful for many other domains as well and as such should not be Nonmem specific. Having such a data-structure would certainly allow to quickly convert Nonmem data to this structure. This is my view on this - and yes we should certainly pool our ideas on the wiki.

BTW, this event-thing could be used to include an event like "new-patient" or better "new grouping unit". This could then potentially in the long run enable a parallelized evaluation of the likelihood (given we figure out how to extend the nested AD to such a case which is doable from my understanding).

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
While we (Charles and I) have built some prototype pharmacometrics (PMX) functions in C++, I'm pretty agnostic about the Stan language vs C++ issue. I agree that certain core functionality should be part of Stan math like numerical solvers for systems of ODEs and algebraic equations and some sort of event handling like that suggested by Sebastian. The more PMX-specific functions could be either C++ or Stan language. I look forward to further discussion about which approach may be optimal or most consistent with Stan design philosophy.

What is missing is some convenient way to distribute and install domain-specific functionality, e.g., some sort of package distribution mechanism ala CRAN or even just being able to include external files containing Stan language functions. In the absence of that, I prefer to have the PMX functions incorporated into Stan so they are easily distributed as part of the standard Stan distribution.

Cheers,
Bill

with the rest of the Stan language because of the recursion
through expressions (or statements).

messages.body_plain:
Most, if not all, scalar and matrix functions are tested with fvar<var> and fvar<fvar<var> > for:

 - valid values
 - invalid values
 - nan values
 - invalid arguments
 - gradients equal expected values
 - function values equal expected values

Most scalar functions and some matrix functions are tested with fvar<var> and fvar<fvar<var> > for:

 - diagonals of hessians vs. expected values
 - diagonals of gradients of hessians vs. expected values

Few, if any, scalar and matrix functions are tested with fvar<var> and fvar<var<var> > for:

 - Full Hessians vs. expected values (and/or finite diff)
 - Gradients of the Hessians vs. expected values (and/or finite diff)

It also looks as if the unit tests in test/unit/math/mix/mat/prob are very sparse and test only that function values equal expected values.

If you need a more full accounting of test inventory, let me know and I/we can write up a file-by-file description.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Re: writing a neural Turing machine in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Autograd's a Python autodiff framework.  So the right level
of comparison, as Dustin points out, would be building something
with our math library in C++, not with the Stan language.  That
is, I think our motivations for Autograd and Stan Math are the
same---autodiffing general programs.  We're working in C++,
whereas Autograd works in Python.  That makes Autograd much more
accessible to most computer science researchers.

Stan's domain-specific language is at a different level of abstraction.
It's a cross-platform tool aimed at doing sampling and optimization and
variational inference in a way that's encapsulated and robust
for applied statisticians.  The target audience for the language is
the same audience as for PyMC's embedded graphical model building
language and for emcee.

Stan's basic approach is more like emcee's---just build a general
density and we'll take it from there.  PyMC, like
BUGS/JAGS/NIMBLE, is directed toward graphical model construction.
This graphical modeling layer is limiting, but also very useful.
By restricting models to be specified with graphical models,
there's a lot of reasoning you can do on the graphical structure
for parallelization, discrete sampling, forward sampling and
posterior predictive checking, automatic likelihood calculations
for cross-validation or WAIC, etc. etc.

I also think there's a lot of latitude for building models modularly
out of full components in something like PyMC that's lacking in Stan.
This is something I haven't seen addressed enough in the probabilistic
programming literature (please send references if you know of any).
A Stan program can include functions, but there's no way to attach another
whole model as a submodel, say as a prior, because there's a mess of global
parameter and data declarations.

The emcee package, on the other hand, is like Stan in taking a general
density as input.  The really flexible thing about emcee is that
it lets you use arbitrary Python programs because it only evaluates
the density with primitive types.  That makes it general enough to deal
with hairy Fortran plugins for scientific forward models (physics, energy usage,
etc.) as well as any old Python code.  They use ensemble sampling methods
which don't need gradients, but also don't mix well in high dimensions.

- Bob

Hi Charles!

Thanks for sharing Torsten. After a first quick look I have the impression that what you did is conceptually very close to what I came up myself. My language to describe things is a bit different (more oriented at the math behind it probably), but the design is the same. I am wondering if we should make the wiki around "complex ODE" models instead of being domain specific on Pharmacometrics. While Pharmacometrics has special needs, these should probably be phrased in more general terms such that other disciplines benefit as well. Given that stan is a general purpose software this would make it a better fit. Another domain where events are used is systems biology and I am sure there are more disciplines.

Is there an example program I can try with Torsten?

One more comment: Out of my own experience in contributing CVODES to the Stan code base, I would advise you to think at the moment about tests, but hold off for the moment to implement all of them. I am saying this as I have myself written lots of tests before there was a definite agreement on design and before I knew where to put things within the Stan source system. As a  result I had to rewrite my tests a few times until I learned where to put stuff and until the design was settled. There were many design aspects which I was not aware of when starting this. This process was at times a bit frustrating for me (no blame on anyone here, I think we are just learning this process), so keep this in mind.

Best,
Sebastian

It’s heavy tailed!  Even though it mostly avoids negative values
every now and then it will have to sojourn out into negative values
to get the right expectations.  If the sampler cannot get sufficiently
out in the tails then the expectation estimators will be biased.  You
can see the sojourns in the trace plot of x.

I spent some time on the plane looking at some chains with many
iterations and things are perhaps a bit weirder still.  2.9.0 is slightly
high in the 5% quantile of x where as 2.10.0 with the fixed step size
is slightly low, but both are consistent with the true value (~0.82).
Still, the histogram for y with the fixed step size in 2.10.0 and 2.9.0
aren’t consistent and I’m guessing the lower quantiles will be even
more different (although it’ll be hard to decouple that from noise).

If this is a heavy-tail issue then it’s going to be really hard to
investigate as noisy estimators will be a generic problem.

Hi Devin,

> Is the listserve the best place to discuss implementation details (I don't think so but don't know where?)

I didn't realize you could not raise issues on a fork -- we'll need a way to redeem this flaw. I would guess using the list-dev is appropriate. You may even consider creating a new conversation, since it might get confusing if all the issues are discussed in this thread. A wiki is a possibility and I may have sharable docs. Proper documentation is also work in progress. A reasonable starting point might be the BUGS model library <https://bitbucket.org/metrumrg/bugsmodellibrary/wiki/Home> which Bill wrote, and which guided a lot of Torsten's development, especially parametrization handling.

Regarding the implementation of the one/two PK model: yes, it does include first-order absorption, the reasoning being that IV dosing is a "special case" where the drug is directly injected in the central compartment. The amount in the first compartment is then 0 all throughout the trial and KA becomes a dummy parameter. I don't believe this results in an important additional computational cost -- though it is something worth testing. We might need a better design if this is confusing.

> This goes in the other direction, like if you have multiple depot compartments for complex absorption models

In this case, I would suggest using the general compartment model, which allows you to write out the ODE system. But there may be more efficient ways to go about this, especially ones that take advantage of the fact we can solve the one and two compartment models analytically. If you have a specific example in mind, we should try to implement a method along those lines.

best,
charles

current understanding of divergences and biases in the
first place!

No sampler parameter changes will fix this — you have
to run the non centered model.  But I like the warnings
— it gives users an immediate taste of how Stan will
yell at you if it sees problems.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for pointing that out, Sebastian.  I agree that
eight schools should work out of the box.

While diagnosing problems is great, I'm afraid potential
users (judging from stories I heard from people at the
ecology conference) are simply concluding that Stan's too hard
and/or broken for models they want.  They don't get that
feeling from JAGS/BUGS, because they don't gripe at users.
So I think we have to somehow work on assuaging user fears long
enough to educate them on why diagnostics are so useful.

We should just change the coding for the eight schools model
here.  I'm OK with providing broken models to users as long
as we also provide fixed ones to go with.

I really don't like eight schools as an intro example
because I found the measurement error aspect of it competely
inscrutable as a beginner.  We also know it's very sensitive
to priors and parameterization.

- Bob

R-based example code (not that I would necessarily envision pre-processing in R, just something easy to make a quick example)

library(purrr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
id_addl <- data_frame(ID = 1:2, time = 0, dose = 100, addl = 8, ii = 12)

addl_to_doses <- function(df) {
  df %>% by_row(function(row) {
    data_frame(DNUM = 0:(row$addl))
  }, .collate="rows") %>%
    mutate(time = time + ii*DNUM) %>%
    select(-.row, -addl, -DNUM)
}
addl_to_doses(id_addl)

Regular dosing patterns allow huge optimizations when you have an analytically solvable system. However, I am not aware of any optimization you can do for the case of ODEs when you subject them to regular dosing.

Best,
Sebastian

You can use analytic things far more often than most people think at least this is my experience so far. Since I have seen running times of 3 days with an ODE and 4h without (same result), I have a clear preference...

I agree about the warnings about divergent transitions and treedepth.  If R-hat indicates poor mixing, then it can be useful to hear about divergent transitions and treedepth.  If mixing is ok, I don't see the advantage of bothering people about transitions and treedepth.

MCSE I'm not sure about.  I had mixed feelings about including it in the default output.  I do like n_eff, though; I think that's pretty intuitive.  In fact, when I explain MCSE now, I explain it by saying it's the posterior sd divided by the sqrt of n_eff.

This new thing I really hate because it always appears, it takes up several lines of output, and it always looks bad.  We're just asking users to say, "Hey, what's wrong, how come these numbers aren't 1, like they should be?"

I think it's fine for this stuff to be available but I think it's bad news for it to be always output.  We're making Stan look less reliable than it is.

Plotting dependence between draws is fine.  I recommend that when R-hat does not go down to 1 after several thousand iterations, users spend some effort trying to figure out what's going on.  But what I see now is settings where we do 2000 iterations, R-hat is around 1.02, n_eff is in the hundreds or thousands, and there are still a few of these messages, just there to give people an unnecessary worry.

No, it really can’t happen.  R-hat is great, but there are lots of pathologies where you
need tens of chains to be sensitive to the problems.  These HMC-specific diagnostics
are super sensitive to these potential problems and identify them long before they
manifest in bad R-hats.

You ignore at your own peril, but you really should be taking these warnings seriously.

> Plotting dependence between draws is fine.  I recommend that when R-hat does not go down to 1 after several thousand iterations, users spend some effort trying to figure out what's going on.  But what I see now is settings where we do 2000 iterations, R-hat is around 1.02, n_eff is in the hundreds or thousands, and there are still a few of these messages, just there to give people an unnecessary worry.

Again, it’s not unnecessary worry.  R-hat is a noisy measure and it doesn’t always
identify pathological behavior quickly enough, especially when the mixing is really
bad.

I’m not sure how actually having information that can identify pathological behavior,
something we get from no other sampler, is bad.  It’s like compiler warnings — you
ignore them at your own peril, but you really really should get in the habit of fixing
them if you want to be building robust models/code.

> Yes, it just happened today.  I had a perfectly well behaved model that had a couple of those divergent transitions or whatever during warmup.  I'd say that _most_ of the models I fit spit out that divergent transitions message, and I mostly fit pretty easy models.

Perfectly well-behaved based on what criteria?  Any divergent iterations indicate
some pathologies are still present and even a few can skew the higher quantiles
significantly.  The right answer is not to ignore them but to increase the step size
and rerun to ensure that you’re covering all the parameter space that needs to
be covered.

Also, any divergent transitions during warmup are not reported so they’d have
to be real problems if you’re seeing them in RStan.

> I'm not saying R-hat is perfect, but currently we're sending so many warnings that I think we're doing little more than bugging people.  And I think it's really really bad to print out things that are .7 .8 .9 and then tell people that ideally these should be 1.  Again, just asking for trouble.

I said it last week and I’ll say it again — we can only hide the real difficulties
with MCMC for so long.  I would not be at all surprised if most of the models
that people fit suffer some small pathologies are hence small (or even large)
biases.  Everyone has just convinced themselves that MCMC should work
without a problem because no other algorithms can identify the problems so
quickly!

Having Rhat, divergences, and the other diagnostics makes us uniquely
suited to ensuring robust fits.  The default should be “expect problems and
tweak the model/settings until they go away” not “problems are rare, my
fit is probably fine and I can ignore all of these warnings”.  Again, this is
not an issue of boy crying wolf, it’s an issue of wolves being everywhere
and we’re only now seeing them.

I’m fine with the next version of RStan putting a threshold on the BFMI,
but at this point that threshold would be entirely heuristic.  We haven’t
developed enough empirical understanding yet to know whether or not
0.7 is okay or could be a sign of something bad.

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

It would be really great to have Stan being able to run in a "quiet" mode which only spits out messages when there is a really bad problem.

Having exposed people in industry to Stan, I can assure you that these Warnings which come out of Stan very often scare people, even though they should just ignore it. I know that education here is the best thing, but not all people who want (or should) use Stan have the time to go into such depth; still MCMC is valuable to their work.

There are just too many false positives right now - a mode which would allow for some false negatives would be beneficial (I am not saying to make this a default!).

Sebastian

> In Stan 2.10 (or maybe it's just rstan 2.10), when you print out the model fit it gives a paragraph about The estimated Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information, along with numbers such as .7 or .9 for each chain.
>
> I have a couple questions here.  First, what is this?  Second, is it a good idea for this to be in the default output?  This seems to be just one more way to get users upset for no reason.  Isn't it enough that we have R-hat?
>
> A

messages.body_plain:
When did everyone get the idea that these are ignorable warnings?
Did everyone forget how many BUGS/JAGS fits we’re seeing were
biased due to the sampler not behaving well?  HMC is better at these
problems but it’s not immune to pathologies, and the huge advantage
that we have over the older algorithms is that we can diagnose the
pathologies in practice!

The only false positive is the occasional Metropolis rejection warning
due to numerical instabilities, and even then it would be best to tweak
the model to avoid the warnings altogether.  The HMC warnings are
_not false positives_.  They indicate real issues.

Remember how problems in the original 8-schools model didn’t show
up until Andy ran HMC for way longer than anyone would reasonable
run it?  These diagnostics find those problems within a reasonable run.
I’m completely overwhelmed by how forgetful everyone seems to be.

Bob — the energy diagnostic is discussed in http://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00695
(I write these papers for a reason!).  There are a collection of examples
demonstrating the utility of this information at the end.  Ultimately the
energy diagnostic is complementary to divergences — whereas divergences
identify light tails that prevent complete sampling, the energy diagnostic
identifies heavy tails that prevent complete sampling.  Heavy tails are
particularly hard problems that can easily sneak around R-hat unless
you run many chains.

Again, we absolutely cannot reinforce the myth that MCMC (or any
computational algorithm) can be run automatically with no validation
of the results.  Statistics is not automatic, and anybody who values
automation over robustness is doomed to their own hubris.

_angry rant over_

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "The estimated Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information is . . ."
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] "The estimated Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information is . . ."
messages.body_plain:
I want to push back against this.  Sure, I think it's fine to leave on _some_ diagnostics by default.  But "The estimated Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information" is not even a diagnostic.  It's something that _every time_, for _every model_, no matter how good, reports numbers less than 1 and then tells the user that these numbers are supposed to be 1.  That's horrible, horrible, horrible!

To put it another way, had we had this conversation a few months earlier, and Bob had said, "we should leave the diagnostics on by default," these diagnostics would not have included "The estimated Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information."  I very strongly oppose this ratcheting in which more and more warnings get spewed out, thus giving people the idea that Stan is fragile.

> On Jul 21, 2016, at 1:40 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> Just to clarify my own position:
>
>  * we should leave the diagnostics on by default
>
>  * we should have examples we can show users that will scare
>    them more than the warnings
>
> Sebastian's right that our users are freaking out and abandoning
> Stan because they interpret the warnings as an indication that
> Stan's broken.   We could let them just go back to
> JAGS and run around bad-mouthing Stan, but I think it would
> be a better service to the field if we could educate people
> with examples they could understand.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>> On Jul 21, 2016, at 9:21 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> When did everyone get the idea that these are ignorable warnings?
>> Did everyone forget how many BUGS/JAGS fits we’re seeing were
>> biased due to the sampler not behaving well?  HMC is better at these
>> problems but it’s not immune to pathologies, and the huge advantage
>> that we have over the older algorithms is that we can diagnose the
>> pathologies in practice!
>>
>> The only false positive is the occasional Metropolis rejection warning
>> due to numerical instabilities, and even then it would be best to tweak
>> the model to avoid the warnings altogether.  The HMC warnings are
>> _not false positives_.  They indicate real issues.
>>
>> Remember how problems in the original 8-schools model didn’t show
>> up until Andy ran HMC for way longer than anyone would reasonable
>> run it?  These diagnostics find those problems within a reasonable run.
>> I’m completely overwhelmed by how forgetful everyone seems to be.
>>
>> Bob — the energy diagnostic is discussed in http://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00695
>> (I write these papers for a reason!).  There are a collection of examples
>> demonstrating the utility of this information at the end.  Ultimately the
>> energy diagnostic is complementary to divergences — whereas divergences
>> identify light tails that prevent complete sampling, the energy diagnostic
>> identifies heavy tails that prevent complete sampling.  Heavy tails are
>> particularly hard problems that can easily sneak around R-hat unless
>> you run many chains.
>>
>> Again, we absolutely cannot reinforce the myth that MCMC (or any
>> computational algorithm) can be run automatically with no validation
>> of the results.  Statistics is not automatic, and anybody who values
>> automation over robustness is doomed to their own hubris.
>>
>> _angry rant over_
>>
>> On Jul 21, 2016, at 3:26 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>> Hi!
>>>
>>> It would be really great to have Stan being able to run in a "quiet" mode which only spits out messages when there is a really bad problem.
>>>
>>> Having exposed people in industry to Stan, I can assure you that these Warnings which come out of Stan very often scare people, even though they should just ignore it. I know that education here is the best thing, but not all people who want (or should) use Stan have the time to go into such depth; still MCMC is valuable to their work.
>>>
>>> There are just too many false positives right now - a mode which would allow for some false negatives would be beneficial (I am not saying to make this a default!).
>>>
>>> Sebastian
>>>
>>> On Wednesday, July 20, 2016 at 6:25:57 PM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>>>> In Stan 2.10 (or maybe it's just rstan 2.10), when you print out the model fit it gives a paragraph about The estimated Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information, along with numbers such as .7 or .9 for each chain.
>>>>
>>>> I have a couple questions here.  First, what is this?  Second, is it a good idea for this to be in the default output?  This seems to be just one more way to get users upset for no reason.  Isn't it enough that we have R-hat?
>>>>
>>>> A

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] "The estimated Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information is . . ."
messages.body_plain:
We have an example in BDA where split R-hat diagnoses the problem but R-hat doesn't.  It's not a real model; I just generated some traceplots that show the problem.  The original example that motivated split R-hat was some model that Ken Shirley was fitting several years ago with 3 chains.  The more chains you have, the less likely you'll need split R-hat.  But with 3 chains, it came in handy.  Also, though, that was an example before we had our current n_eff measure that combines between and within-chain information.  We used to use a n_eff measure that only used between-chain info, and that was very noisy.  I think split R-hat and the new n_eff catch a lot.

data simulation checks) as they all provide unique
views into potential problems.

On Monday, July 25, 2016 at 9:46:38 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, yes, I agree that I would not stop when R-hat is 1.2.  I'm just curious:  in this particular example are there some parameters where the inferences are way off?

It is real data so we don't know what the true values are. We do know that the intercepts are systematically different across chains despite the Rhats being 1.00 to 1.02. The Rhat for lp__ is a bit like the BFMI in that it depends on all the margins. But we have tended to say not to worry about the Rhat for lp__ because the marginal distribution of lp__ tends to be not normal. The BFMI being <= 0.3 was the most obvious numerical indicator of danger.

Ben

There will certainly be a strong overlap between strong autocorrelations in lp__
and a small BFMI (maybe we should call it E-BFMI to specify that it’s the BFMI
of the energy transitions?), but the overlap isn’t complete so there is useful
information in both.  Ultimately the E-BFMI most readily identifies the heavy-tailed
distributions which may obstruct geometric ergodicity and hence for which we cannot
trust the MCSE.  This looks like an excellent example of that behavior.

messages.body_plain:
I finally found out what's causing numerical issues. Turns out that starting from a value that's not identical to the old one (down to the last bit) causes the results to be fairly different.

On the unconstrained space, the old one initialized the one unconstrained parameter to:
1.5641332541198749

The buggy one initialized it to:
1.5641332541198751

That was enough to send everything off the rails.

I was getting that due to initializing on the unconstrained space, creating a var_context on the constrained space using transforms, then letting the inverse transform get it back to the unconstrained space.

I eliminated that step, so we're good again.

That took way too long to find.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
The intro needs to be stronger.  We need to make it absolutely clear that
no statistical algorithm is guaranteed to get the right results on all models
and care is always needed.  This is especially confusing for MCMC which
is always quoted as being “unbiased” — but this is true only when you can
run the chains infinitely long.  Whether or not MCMC yields good values
in finite time is a much more challenging problem.

Also, it’s not just a design choice on our part that we show more diagnostics.
We _have_ more diagnostics to show.  This is a huge _feature_, not some
arbitrary choice.

I hate people taking the “particle moving through the distribution” analogy
too seriously.  I think it’s much clearer to say something like “the step size
controls the resolution of the sampler — for particularly hard problems
there are features of the target distribution that are too small for this
resolution.  Consequently the sampler misses those features and returns
biased estimates.  Fortunately, this mismatch of scales manifests as
_divergences_ which provide a practical diagnostic.”

As for recommendations, the increased adapt_delta will work only when
there are a few, say O(1%), divergences.  If there are many more then
there are modeling problems.  Either the model is wrong or a serious
reparameterization is needed.

In the Metropolis section we need to add that the user should check
that the support of their parameters matches the distributions.

Regarding workflow, this is the workflow I recommend in my tutorials:

Everything else is just some tweak of an ANOVA-like test or
a measure of autocorrelation.  Without having sampler-specific
information this is literally all the Markov chain provides that
can be tested.  Rhat wins over other ANOVA-like test that I’ve
ever seen (the multiple chains being critical) whereas the
autocorrelation measures are all limited by interpretability,
at least in my opinion.

Again, the novel thing in the HMC diagnostics is that they
are direct diagnostics on the _interaction_ of the sampler
and the target distribution, and not just an obfuscated
manifestation of that interaction.

On Wednesday, July 27, 2016 at 1:15:14 PM UTC-4, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> Ok, I've incorporated Michael and Sebastian's advice. There's an updated version here, and I'm happy to keep making changes if people have more comments or don't like any of what I just added.

This part: "While reading this document it is important to keep in mind that there is no statistical algorithm that is guaranteed to get the right results on all models. Markov chain Monte Carlo is no exception. Although it is often advertised as being “unbiased”, this is not a guarantee unless the Markov chains are infinitely long. Whether or not MCMC yields good values in finite time is a much more challenging problem."

Could be something like: "While reading this document it is important to keep in mind that there is no statistical algorithm that is guaranteed to get the right results on all models. [Optimization can get stuck in local modes and even a simple linear regression can give nonsense answers in the presence of colinearity.] Markov chain Monte Carlo is no exception. Although it is often advertised as being “unbiased”, this is not a guarantee unless the Markov chains are infinitely long. Whether or not MCMC yields good values in finite time is a much more challenging problem."

The maximum tree depth could give a rough idea of how much memory Stan will suck up with increasing depth.  I don't recall off hand... [number of parameters]*2^treedepth (?)

Should there be a section about the BFMI? I feel like we lack guidance about the exact cut-off but we could give an example for when it is low and why it's low (something from Michael's write-up would be fine).  For example this snippet gives low BFMI:

library(rstan); stan(model_code='parameters { real x;} model { x ~ cauchy(0,1);}')

The BFMI's are near .3 and we know that it's an example that runs and gives fine R-hats but doesn't give correct quantiles.  The current warning seems to be the worst-case where we give an ominous warning with no context.

messages.subject: CmdStan v2.11.0 released! Please upgrade from v2.10.0.
messages.subject_clean: CmdStan v2.11.0 released! Please upgrade from v2.10.0.
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

CmdStan v2.11.0 was released today: https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/releases/tag/v2.11.0

There was a bug in sampling introduced in Stan v2.10.0 (stan-dev/stan#1972 <https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1972>) that was fixed for this version. We suggest upgrading from v2.10.0 to v2.11.0 immediately.

For users of Stan.jl, MatlabStan, or StataStan, upgrading the underlying CmdStan installation will be sufficient.

RStan and PyStan will be patched and released soon.

> On Jul 27, 2016, at 1:15 PM, Jonah Sol Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Ok, I've incorporated Michael and Sebastian's advice. There's an updated version here, and I'm happy to keep making changes if people have more comments or don't like any of what I just added.
>
> Seth, I know the warning you're referring to, but haven't come across it in a while. If you have a small example that'd be great.
>
> Jonah
>
> On Wed, Jul 27, 2016 at 11:56 AM, Jonah Sol Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Wed, Jul 27, 2016 at 4:27 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> The intro needs to be stronger.  We need to make it absolutely clear that
> no statistical algorithm is guaranteed to get the right results on all models
> and care is always needed.  This is especially confusing for MCMC which
> is always quoted as being “unbiased” — but this is true only when you can
> run the chains infinitely long.  Whether or not MCMC yields good values
> in finite time is a much more challenging problem.
>
> Ok I'll make it more forceful.
>
>
> Also, it’s not just a design choice on our part that we show more diagnostics.
> We _have_ more diagnostics to show.  This is a huge _feature_, not some
> arbitrary choice.
>
> Yes, good point. I'll emphasize that diagnostics (e.g. divergences) are unique to HMC,
> although the problems they indicate are not.
>
> I hate people taking the “particle moving through the distribution” analogy
> too seriously.
>
> Ok, I don't take it too seriously but I do like to have some sort of analogy. I think
> you've used planetary motion in some of your presentations. How about that one?
> Or I just skip the analogies and just link to one of your talks?
>
> I think it’s much clearer to say something like “the step size
> controls the resolution of the sampler — for particularly hard problems
> there are features of the target distribution that are too small for this
> resolution.  Consequently the sampler misses those features and returns
> biased estimates.  Fortunately, this mismatch of scales manifests as
> _divergences_ which provide a practical diagnostic.”
>
> Ok, nice. I'll use this.
>
>
> As for recommendations, the increased adapt_delta will work only when
> there are a few, say O(1%), divergences.  If there are many more then
> there are modeling problems.  Either the model is wrong or a serious
> reparameterization is needed.
>
> In the Metropolis section we need to add that the user should check
> that the support of their parameters matches the distributions.
>
> Ok will add.
>
> Thanks for comments!
>
>
